g.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a
powerful paradigm for training reasoning models (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025;
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=2) Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training reasoning models (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024).

g.text: RLVR uses verifiers vs preference models
Unlike traditional RLHF that relies on learned preference models, RLVR uses
automated verifiers to provide reward signals by comparing model responses
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) Unlike traditional RLHF that relies on learned preference models, RLVR uses automated verifiers to provide reward signals by comparing model responses against ground-truth reference answers.

g.text: This approach has enabled significant advances in mathematical reasoning and
other domains where correctness can be objectively verified.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) This approach has enabled significant advances in mathematical reasoning and other domains where correctness can be objectively verified.

g.text: However, reference-based verifiers harbor a critical
vulnerability: they can be fooled by trivial "master-key"
responses that exploit reference answer leakage (Zhao et al.,
g.title: N4 [Limitation] (cites=1) However, reference-based verifiers harbor a critical vulnerability: they can be fooled by trivial "master-key" responses that exploit reference answer leakage (Zhao et al., 2025).

g.text: These master keys—single tokens like ":" or short phrases like
"Thought process:"—contain no substantive answer yet achieve false
positive verification rates of 25–29% on state-of-the-art
verifiers including xVerify (Chen et al., 2025) and…
g.title: N5 [Result] (cites=2) These master keys—single tokens like ":" or short phrases like "Thought process:"—contain no substantive answer yet achieve false positive verification rates of 25–29% on state-of-the-art verifiers including xVerify (Chen et al., 2025) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024).

g.text: Corrupts RLVR via reward hacking and collapse
Such vulnerabilities can corrupt RLVR training by rewarding
non-solutions, potentially leading to reward hacking and training
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) Such vulnerabilities can corrupt RLVR training by rewarding non-solutions, potentially leading to reward hacking and training collapse.

g.text: Simple defenses like length filtering fail against sentence-length master
keys, with worst-case false positive rates remaining at 28.87%.
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) Simple defenses like length filtering fail against sentence-length master keys, with worst-case false positive rates remaining at 28.87%.

g.text: Need defenses on deeper semantic properties
This motivates the need for defenses that operate on deeper semantic
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) This motivates the need for defenses that operate on deeper semantic properties rather than surface features.

g.text: We propose RefSwap, a training-free method that detects master-key attacks
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) We propose RefSwap, a training-free method that detects master-key attacks through counterfactual reference swapping.

g.text: The key insight is that legitimate correct responses exhibit self-solving
behavior—the verifier can recognize correctness even with mismatched
references—while master-key false positives cannot self-solve because they
g.title: N10 [Method: insight] (cites=0) The key insight is that legitimate correct responses exhibit self-solving behavior—the verifier can recognize correctness even with mismatched references—while master-key false positives cannot self-solve because they contain no actual answer.

g.text: By sampling multiple counterfactual references and computing the
maximum verification probability (max p cf), RefSwap achieves
near-perfect separation between true positives and master-key
g.title: N11 [Result] (cites=0) By sampling multiple counterfactual references and computing the maximum verification probability (max p cf), RefSwap achieves near-perfect separation between true positives and master-key false positives (AUC=0.991).

g.text: We identify and quantify the master-key vulnerability
in RLVR verifiers, showing 25–29% false positive rates
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We identify and quantify the master-key vulnerability in RLVR verifiers, showing 25–29% false positive rates on state-of-the-art systems.

g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose Multi-CF RefSwap, a training-free detection method using max p cf scoring that exploits the self-solving asymmetry between true positives and master keys.

g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate 96.8% relative FPR reduction (25.50%→0.81%) on xVerify-7B-I with only 2.74pp accuracy cost, uniformly neutralizing all 10 tested master keys.

g.title: C4 [Contribution] (cites=0) We analyze backbone dependency, revealing that verifier architecture determines susceptibility to counterfactual-based detection.
